catalog_quote: 6.1.3 Prosodische Erscheinungen Es handelt sich um Vokallänge und Tonhöhe. Alle Vokale außer /a/ können lang und kurz auftreten. Über Konsonantenlänge (geminiertes /t/) vgl. Anm. 2. Zu unterscheiden sind nach den bisherigen Beobachtungen ein hoher, ein tiefer und ein fallender Ton. Tonologische Regeln können jedoch nicht angegeben werden. 6.2 Morphophonologie 6.2.1 Konsonanten ... [Anmerkungen zu Kapitel 6, Anm. 1:] ... notiert. Auf Grund meiner Daten scheint die Zuordnung dieses Lautes zu /d/ weitgehend gerechtfertigt, aber nicht problemlos. Weitere Unterschiede zu Heines Darstellung sind: a) Ich habe keine Druckakzente notiert. b) Ich habe häufiger Auslautvokale angegeben, wo Heines Notierung konsonantisch endet. c) Vokalfolgen bei Heine entsprechen in meiner Notierung Folgen mit Halbvokal. Vgl. (Heine) /moUta/ : (Rottland) /mowta/ ...

new_statements.translation: 6.1.3 Prosodic phenomena. These are vowel length and pitch. All vowels except /a/ can occur long and short. On consonant length (geminated /t/) see note 2. According to the observations so far, a high, a low and a falling tone are to be distinguished. Tonological rules, however, cannot be given. ... [ch. 6 note 1:] Further differences from Heine's presentation are: a) I have not recorded any stress accents. b) I have more often given final vowels where Heine's notation ends in a consonant.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Omotik is described as a tone language (high, low, falling) with distinctive vowel length; the describer treats length and pitch as the only prosodic phenomena and explicitly recorded no stress accent, in contrast to Heine 1973, whose Omotik wordlist marks a 'Druckakzent' word by word (apostrophe before the stressed vowel) without stating any placement rule. No source gives a position for word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (For the sister branch Kalenjin, same book 5.1.3.2 pp.77-78: no phonemic stress; phonetically stressed syllables always bear non-low tone; in Heine's Sogoo list stress co-occurs with high or falling tone 'but is otherwise not predictable'.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level transcription of elicited lexical/grammatical material from the last rememberers (main informant Noontirinya, also Heine's 1973 informant); language moribund at the time; statement concerns isolated words, no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Omotik = Laamoot (self-name laamoot, sg. olamooti), ISO omt, Glottolog omot1239 (dialect node Suiei suie1242 listed under it). Rottland's 1976-78 data and Heine's 1973 list come from the same main informant (Noontirinya) among Maasai near Lolgorien/Lemek, Narok District; the language was already moribund (a few elderly rememberers), so both descriptions rest on elicited words from semi-speakers. Not to be confused with Afroasiatic 'Omotic'.

sources.note: Sec. 6.1.3 (complete, reconstructed verbatim from three overlapping snippets): Omotik prosodic phenomena are vowel length and pitch; high, low and falling tone distinguished; no tonological rules can be given. Ch. 6 note 1 (p.152): unlike Heine 1973, 'Ich habe keine Druckakzente notiert' (I recorded no stress accents). For Kalenjin (5.1.3.2, pp.77-78) the same author says stress has no phonemic function and phonetically stressed syllables always carry non-low tone.
Stub; cites only Ethnologue; no phonology.
